name: StressDream (steered world-model policy evaluation)
modality: Policy actions + current observation fed to a diffusion video world model (Vista for driving, Ctrl-World for manipulation); initial noise is optimized with a VLM semantic objective plus a plausibility objective to steer imagined futures toward text-specified high-impact events (e.g. task failure, collision); policies scored by whether plausible steered futures contain the undesirable outcome.
what_it_measures: Whether a policy's actions admit plausible failure futures under a video world model, used for robust offline policy evaluation and for weighting fine-tuning data. Measures recall of failure events found per imagination budget and downstream policy success after robust fine-tuning.
size: Driving: 100 image-action-text pairs across 8 safety-critical event categories plus 200 imminent-collision examples. Manipulation: 6 contact-rich tasks, ~150 teleop trajectories per task, 100 failure trajectories for evaluation, 40 successful demos per task for fine-tuning. Plus a Dubins-car controlled study.
reported_metrics: Failure-event recall 54% to 94% vs nominal sampling (manipulation); pi0.5 VLA success 39% to 71% after robust fine-tuning; Dubins car: high TPR while keeping high TNR (steers to failure only when plausible).
cost_evidence: 20 noise-optimization steps (driving) and 10 (manipulation) per imagination; authors note current WMs take several minutes per imagination; Vista noise dim ~922K, Ctrl-World ~58K. No GPU-hour total stated.
validity_evidence: Dubins-car ground truth shows steering finds failures only when dynamically plausible; manipulation failures judged by human labelling of generated videos; driving quality checked with WorldModelBench. Authors state plausibility is limited to what the WM supports and does not imply physical plausibility; no real-robot rollouts confirm predicted failures.
notes: Most directly eval-centric Bajcsy paper. Co-authored with Marco Pavone (also a SPAIS speaker link). Code: https://github.com/CMU-IntentLab/StressDream, project page https://junwon.me/StressDream/ (both fetched, 200). Venue CoRL 2026 per lab publications page.

name: Regret metric for system-level prediction failures (Not All Errors Are Made Equal)
modality: Closed-loop human-robot interaction logs (predictor + planner) scored offline by a probabilistic, calibrated regret: the gap between the planner's realized closed-loop performance and what it would have achieved with the true human trajectory. Compared to open-loop ADE/FDE and other system-level metrics.
what_it_measures: Which trajectory-prediction errors actually degraded closed-loop robot behavior (system-level failures), and whether mining high-regret interactions is predictive of re-deployment performance improvement after fine-tuning.
size: 96 closed-loop 20-second driving scenarios (BITS simulator, nuScenes-initialized, AgentFormer predictor, TPP planner): 20 high-regret, 76 low-regret. Hardware: LoCoBot social navigation with a VQ-VAE generative planner trained on 10k synthetic trajectories.
reported_metrics: Generalized regret has 95% overlap with canonical regret but only 35% overlap with ADE-flagged failures; fine-tuning on the 23% high-regret subset gives -65% collision cost and -53% closed-loop regret on high-regret scenarios, competitive with full-data fine-tuning; ADE/FDE 0.327/1.520 vs base 0.371/1.919; hardware regret 0.307 on near-collision vs 0.053-0.078 nominal.
cost_evidence: 96 simulated scenarios and a small number of hardware trials; fine-tuning on 23% of data matches full-data fine-tuning (data efficiency claim). No compute hours stated.
validity_evidence: Presence of high-regret data during fine-tuning is 'highly predictive' of re-deployment improvement; hardware trials show high regret on interactions with unexpectedly close human-robot proximity. Correlation with actual collisions is shown through collision-cost reduction, not accident statistics.
notes: Semantic Scholar also lists a 2024 arXiv title 'A General Calibrated Regret Metric for Detecting and Mitigating Human-Robot Interaction Failures'; this appears to be an earlier version title of the same arXiv ID (v1-v4), not a separate paper. Project page https://cmu-intentlab.github.io/not-all-errors/ and code fetched (200).

name: Safety observability / predictability diagnostics for latent world models (MultiSafe)
modality: Latent world model trained on robot observation-action data; two diagnostics score the model: (1) mutual-information-based safety observability between observations and safety labels (Barber-Agakov bound), (2) rollout-based future safety predictability (failure-classification accuracy over 16-step open-loop rollouts). Downstream latent safety filter evaluated on hardware.
what_it_measures: Whether a world model's latent state carries the information needed to detect and anticipate safety violations under partial observability (estimation gaps vs prediction gaps), and how much mitigation (multimodal supervision, conformal risk calibration) recovers safety on real cooking-like tasks.
size: 2 hardware tasks on Franka Research 3 (wax heating with IR camera, rice pouring with GelSight tactile); 20 trials per method (wax), 50 filled + 50 empty bottle trials (rice); training data 180 (wax) and 650 (rice) teleop trajectories.
reported_metrics: Wax: RGB-only filter lifts pot safely 15% [CI 0.04-0.39] vs multimodal 100% [0.80-1.0]; normalized MI wax RGB 0.221 vs IR 0.801, rice RGB 0.962 vs tactile 0.221; rice: RGB-only pours 14% of filled bottles at target alpha 0.12, multimodal 14% filled / 60% empty.
cost_evidence: 20-100 hardware trials per condition; WM training 20k iterations, safety filter 600k DDPG iterations; sensors: FLIR Lepton IR, Intel D415, Zed Mini, GelSight Mini. No wall-clock stated.
validity_evidence: Diagnostics computed offline are shown to predict which sensing configuration yields safe hardware behavior (low MI for RGB matches 15% success; high MI for IR matches 100%). Sample sizes small (20-50 trials) with reported confidence intervals.
notes: arXiv posted Oct 2025; lab page lists CoRL 2026. Project page https://cmu-intentlab.github.io/multisafe/ fetched (200). The diagnostics are reusable as an offline test of whether a safety filter's sensing suite is sufficient.

name: Position: embodied reward models need bad behavior data (RoboArena reward-model audit)
modality: Real-robot rollout videos with human preference rankings and 0-100 scores (RoboArena) fed to three embodied reward models (ReWiND, GVL with GPT-5, Dopamine); scored by preference-ordering accuracy against human evaluators, stratified by task category.
what_it_measures: How well embodied reward models agree with human judgments of real robot behavior, and where they over-reward unsafe, poorly executed, or shortcut behaviors; the effect of adding real bad-behavior data.
size: 723 valid RoboArena tasks with 2-6 rollouts each (427 pick/place, 32 push/pull, 72 open/close, 47 stack, 68 reorient, 30 pour, 47 tool use).
reported_metrics: Preference-ordering accuracy 0.72-0.77 on pick/place falling to 0.52-0.62 on tool use (chance 0.50); in-context injection of bad data gives ~10% accuracy gain for GVL on hard tasks.
cost_evidence: Relies on RoboArena's existing decentralized real-robot evaluation with human labels; paper argues negative data is costly to collect and often withheld. No own compute stated.
validity_evidence: Ground truth is human evaluator preference on real robot rollouts; agreement rates reported per category.
notes: Explicitly calls for decentralized physical evaluation systems and fine-grained reward-model benchmarks. Directly relevant to the value of human-labelled safety evaluations.

name: Rethinking Safety for Generalist Robots (embodied AI safety agenda)
modality: No system under test; taxonomy of risks (contextual hazards, misalignment, adversarial actors) and a full-stack research agenda including evaluation.
what_it_measures: Nothing empirically. Argues real-world safety testing is 'unsafe by definition, time-consuming, and costly', so safety cases must combine QA benchmarks, high-fidelity simulation or world models, and statistically rigorous finite hardware trials; calls for severity-stratified, automatically scorable safety metrics, continuous evaluation, and robotics red-teaming.
cost_evidence: States real-world safety evaluation is costly and unsafe; motivates offline evaluation and combining large imperfect offline tests with limited real trials.
validity_evidence: none stated; identifies sim-to-real trustworthiness of tests as the central open challenge.
notes: Posted Sept 2026. The most directly quotable framing for a value-of-information argument about safety evals. Companion talk 'What Does Safety Mean for Generalist Robots?' (Georgia Tech IRIM seminar, Aug 2026) is a seminar, not a paper.

name: LIBERO-100-R / LIBERO-10-R OOD evaluation suite (Do What You Say)
modality: Reasoning VLA receives language instruction and images in LIBERO simulation; evaluation suite adds reasoning annotations to LIBERO-100 demos plus 4 OOD perturbation types (Lang-Rephrase, Lang-Object-Property, Visual-Scene, Visual-Viewpoint); scored by task success rate over 50 trials per task.
what_it_measures: Embodied chain-of-thought faithfulness: whether executed actions match the VLA's own textual plan under semantic and visual distribution shift; also behavior-composition generalization.
size: LIBERO-10 tasks x 4 perturbation types; 50 trials per task; three dataset scales (LIBERO-10-R, LIBERO-100-Basket-R, LIBERO-100-R). Hardware demos also reported.
reported_metrics: Up to 15% success gain over prior work on behavior-composition tasks; gains scale with samples and data diversity.
cost_evidence: Training ~20 h on 8 A100; inference 347 ms at K=10 samples; GPT-4o verification 7-10 s per query.
validity_evidence: none stated beyond simulation success; OOD suite is synthetic perturbation of LIBERO.
notes: Released artifacts: https://github.com/NVlabs/Libero-10-r (fetched 200), dataset on HuggingFace nvidia/libero-r-datasets. Robustness rather than safety benchmark; included because the OOD suite is reusable and released.

name: Conformalized language steering with LIBERO-OOD harmlessness evaluation
modality: Frozen pi0.5 VLA in LIBERO-OOD (10 tasks x 4 visual conditions x 5 semantic variants = 200 combinations) and Franka hardware; a conformalized improvement head decides when to intervene; scored by success rate and false-positive (harmful) intervention rate at alpha=0.10.
what_it_measures: Whether a runtime steering intervention improves a VLA without harming it OOD; conformal guarantee P(intervene | steering harmful) <= alpha.
size: Sim: 200 task-perturbation combinations, 50 rollouts each, 10 calibration episodes per condition over 5 splits. Hardware: 4 seen + 2 novel tasks, 30 rollouts per condition, 20 calibration samples per perturbation.
reported_metrics: +24.7% success in sim, +65.0% on hardware in-distribution; harmful-intervention FPR 38.92% to 9.31% (sim) and 61.11% to 2.22% (hardware) after conformalization.
cost_evidence: NVIDIA A6000 Ada; +68 ms per replanning cycle (14.7 Hz to 9.8 Hz); tens of thousands of sim rollouts; ~30 hardware rollouts per condition.
validity_evidence: Conformal coverage checked empirically on held-out perturbations; hardware FPR matches target alpha.
notes: Included as a clearly described reusable protocol (calibration split + perturbation grid + harm-rate metric), not as a safety benchmark per se.

name: UNISafe OOD-failure evaluation of latent safety filters
modality: Vision-based control (RGB) through a latent world model; safety filter classifies states safe/unsafe with epistemic uncertainty (Jensen-Renyi divergence) calibrated by conformal prediction; scored by TPR/TNR/balanced accuracy vs ground-truth failure sets, and by failure rate, safe-success rate, incompletion rate in closed loop, including replayed failure trajectories on hardware.
what_it_measures: Whether a latent safety filter detects both known and unseen (OOD) hazards, and the safety/conservativeness tradeoff versus baselines (LatentSafe, SafeOnly, CQL/COMBO, density estimation, total uncertainty).
size: Dubins car: 181 challenging initial states, 1000 safe + 50 random training trajectories. IsaacLab block plucking: 1000 sampled initial conditions, 3000 training trajectories. Hardware Jenga (Franka Research 3): 720 training trajectories (150 random, 480 success, 90 failure), 50 replayed failure trajectories.
reported_metrics: Block plucking: UNISafe safe-success 0.72, failure 0.20, incompletion 8% vs LatentSafe 0.68/0.30/1% vs no filter 0.58/0.41.
cost_evidence: Trajectory counts above; DDQN/SAC solvers; no compute hours stated. Code and IsaacLab demo released.
validity_evidence: Grid-based ground-truth reachability on Dubins car; hardware failure replays only (50), not statistically large.
notes: Method paper; included because the OOD-failure replay protocol and metrics are explicit and code is public (https://cmu-intentlab.github.io/UNISafe/, fetched 200).

name: SALT runtime monitor evaluation (Robots that Suggest Safe Alternatives)
modality: Goal-conditioned imitation policy monitored by a goal-parameterized reach-avoid value network; monitor scored as binary classifier (TPR/TNR/FPR/FNR/F1) of closed-loop success vs failure against exhaustive gridding or sampled rollouts; user study rates acceptability of suggested alternative goals.
what_it_measures: Whether a closed-loop reachability monitor predicts execution failures better than open-loop uncertainty quantification (ensemble disagreement), and whether suggested alternatives match human preferences.
size: Navigation: exhaustive 50x50x20x20 state grid; manipulation (Robosuite Franka Panda): 1000 initial (s,g) pairs x 10 seeds; user study with 20 expert participants at CMU and UCSD.
reported_metrics: Navigation TPR 37.34%, FNR 4.38% (SALT) vs ensemble TPR 1.92%, RewardSum FNR 35.78%; alternative alignment with humans 70-100%.
validity_evidence: Ground truth from simulated closed-loop rollouts; human agreement on alternatives; no hardware.

name: Unifying AV safety concepts via HJ reachability (RSS, SFF comparison)
org: Stanford ASL / UC Berkeley (Bajcsy with Pavone group)
modality: Existing AV safety concepts (Responsibility-Sensitive Safety, NVIDIA Safety Force Field, others) embedded in a common HJ reachability formulation; proposes data-driven synthesis of safety concepts and safety-centric dataset construction (querying humans for safety labels, coverage of safety-critical scenarios under a labeling budget).
what_it_measures: No empirical evaluation; a framework for comparing what different AV safety concepts flag as unsafe, plus research directions on safety-critical dataset construction and interpretable safety representations.
cost_evidence: Discusses limited labeling budgets and the need for dataset coverage of safety-critical scenarios; no numbers.
notes: Bajcsy and Leung equal contribution; co-authored with Marco Pavone (also a SPAIS speaker). Earlier title 'Towards the Unification and Data-Driven Synthesis of Autonomous Vehicle Safety Concepts' (v1). PDF text confirmed sections on safety-centric dataset construction.

name: Confidence-aware game-theoretic safety monitor evaluated on INTERACTION dataset
modality: HJ backward reachable tube (BRT) safety monitor with Bayesian confidence over game-theoretic human models; evaluated in simulated merging/roundabout/highway interactions and by replaying real human driving pairs; scored by safety-controller activation count, reward improvement percent, over-conservatism percentage (BRT area vs least-conservative BRT) and BRT violation percentage on real data.
what_it_measures: How conservative a runtime safety monitor is relative to real human driving, and whether confidence-aware models cut interventions without collisions.
size: 200 pairwise interactions extracted from the INTERACTION dataset; simulated roundabout and highway scenarios; ablations with unmodeled distracted humans.
reported_metrics: ~20% fewer safety-controller activations than full BRT in roundabout while collision-free; +27.75% reward vs full BRT; +9.18% vs lambda-only BRT under misspecification; ~29% reward gain over no-game variant; over-conservatism and violation percentages both significantly reduced vs full BRT on real data.
validity_evidence: Real human driving replays show humans violate the proposed monitor's constraints less often than the full BRT, i.e. the monitor is closer to observed human safety margins.
notes: Bajcsy is equal-contribution co-first author. The real-data conservatism metric (fraction of real interactions a monitor would flag as unsafe) is a reusable proxy evaluation for runtime monitors.

name: Reachability-based analysis of online-adapting human models
modality: The robot's online learning algorithm for a parameterized human model is treated as a dynamical system whose control is the human data; dynamic programming computes the set of hypotheses learnable in finite time and best/worst-case learning times; scored analytically, no real data.
what_it_measures: Safety-relevant properties of a human predictor: what it could learn online, how fast (worst/best case), and which initializations guarantee finite-time convergence; applied to driving intersection, confidence-aware navigation, legible/deceptive navigation, gradient-based reward learning.
size: 4 simulated domains; low-dimensional parameter spaces only.
reported_metrics: Driving: correct branching time cuts distance-to-goal 6.88 m to 3.42 m while safe; confidence-detection best-case 0.9-2.72 s; learning time <=2.2 s vs ~4.7 s by initialization.
cost_evidence: Dynamic programming over discrete or 2D continuous parameter spaces; does not scale beyond low dimensions.
validity_evidence: none stated; no real human data.
notes: Code https://github.com/abajcsy/pred_analyzer fetched (200). An offline verification/analysis tool rather than an empirical eval.

name: Human-AI Safety: control-systems view of AI safety (position)
modality: No system under test; formalism for dynamic human-AI feedback loops and a technical roadmap.
what_it_measures: Nothing empirically; argues safety assurances must reason about closed-loop human-AI dynamics rather than fine-tuning outputs in isolation.
notes: Adjacent framing only; not an evaluation.

name: ReGuard control-theoretic guardrail evaluation (From Refusal to Recovery)
modality: LLM agents (Llama-3.x, GPT-4o/4o-mini/GPT-5, Qwen2.5-72B) acting in simulated planar driving, WebArena shopping with a $50 budget, and a backseat-driver advice setting; guardrail trained by safety-critical RL in the model's latent space; scored by success rate, failure (collision/bankruptcy) rate, value F1, intervention rate vs flag-and-block (LlamaGuard) baselines.
what_it_measures: Whether predictive guardrails prevent catastrophic downstream outcomes of agentic AI while preserving task performance, compared with refusal-based guardrails.
size: 3 simulated domains; 7 LLM agents; episode counts not extracted.
reported_metrics: Driving: ReGuard 77.3% success / 18.8% failure vs 44.4% / 55.6% myopic baseline, value F1 0.99; commerce: 87.5% success matching GPT-4o vs 62.5% zero-shot Llama; backseat driving success 44.9% to 64.2% with 62.1% intervention rate.
cost_evidence: Training 66 h (RTX 4090, driving), 150 h (RTX 4090, commerce), 80 h (RTX A6000 Ada, backseat).
notes: Not a robot per se (LLM agent in toy driving sim); included as adjacent because the guardrail-vs-refusal comparison protocol with explicit compute cost is reusable.

name: Conformal Decision Theory pedestrian-navigation risk evaluation
modality: Robot planner around pedestrians replayed from the Stanford Drone Dataset (nexus_4 scene); a conformal controller adapts a risk parameter online; scored by safety violations against a 2 m distance threshold and time-to-goal versus aggressive, conservative and ACI baselines.
what_it_measures: Whether decisions calibrated directly by conformal risk control achieve a target long-run risk without distributional assumptions, and at what efficiency cost.
size: One SDD scene (nexus_4) with dense pedestrians; plus stock trading and manufacturing case studies.
reported_metrics: 0 safety violations at learning rate eta>=100; time-to-goal 17.4 s vs ACI 26.67 s (~29% faster) vs unsafe aggressive 8.57 s; min distance 1.142 m.
validity_evidence: Replay of real pedestrian trajectories; statistical risk guarantee is assumption-free but evaluated on a single scene.
notes: Bajcsy equal-contribution co-first author. Adjacent; the evaluation is small.

name: HJ reachability analysis of prior misspecification in human motion prediction
modality: Human motion predictor cast as HJ reachability over joint human state and belief over model parameters; compared against worst-case forward reachable sets and a Bayesian stochastic predictor in simulation and quadrotor hardware; scored by robustness of the resulting plan under incorrect priors and by conservatism.
what_it_measures: The effect of incorrect priors/observation models on future human-state predictions and on the safety of the resulting robot plan.
size: Simulation plus hardware demonstrations; trial counts not extracted.
reported_metrics: Qualitative: robust yet not overly conservative planning even when the human model is inaccurate.
notes: Bajcsy equal-contribution co-first author. Analysis method rather than an evaluation; borderline.

name: Latent Safety Filters (latent-space HJ reachability) hardware protocol
modality: RGB observations through a generative world model; failure set specified as a latent-space classifier trained on mixed-quality data (successes, random exploration, unsafe demos); filter shields arbitrary policies (IL and teleop) on a Franka Research 3; scored by prevented failures (bag spilling, toppling clutter) in simulation and hardware.
what_it_measures: Whether a learned latent reachability filter prevents hard-to-specify failures on a real manipulator while preserving task completion.
size: Simulation and hardware experiments; 7 tables and 9 figures per arXiv comment; trial counts not extracted.
notes: Foundational method paper for the latent-safety line; included for context only. Code https://kensukenk.github.io/latent-safety/ fetched (200).
